r3-p13-016: On bridge E, the peak at about 1.74 Hz stood clearly above the noise and was tracked stably in every session over the four days, with differences between sessions below 1%. The uncompensated false-alarm rate when one session's threshold was applied to another stayed mostly at or below 2%, even after remounting.
r3-p13-017: No benefit from temperature/humidity compensation appeared. When the temperature ranges of training and evaluation overlapped, all four models had the same false-alarm rate of about 1–2%, and when the evaluation temperature fell outside the training range, the compensated models' false-alarm rates actually increased. Controlling for traffic amplitude within the same mounting period (air temperature about 15–39 °C), the estimated temperature slope of the peak frequency was indistinguishable from zero. With an openLAB-level temperature effect (−0.19%/°C), the peak should have dropped by about 4.5% over the 24 °C range, but the measurements were flat throughout (Figure 6). The peak change implied by the measured slope was about 0.5%, at the level of the fluctuation between 5-minute blocks. An amplitude dependence — the peak falling slightly as traffic amplitude rose — was more pronounced.
r3-p13-018: The exceeding windows did not come from temperature either. Exceedances concentrated in the evening and late night, when traffic was light, especially in low-amplitude windows, and a sensor error that logs zeros on all three axes occurred intermittently on both bridges (about 10% of E's records; those windows were excluded from analysis). In the preliminary measurement on bridge C (three sessions with the same mounting on September 20, about 6 hours), the 3.81 Hz mode peak chosen in the screening measurement was reproduced in every session, and because an adjacent peak also appeared, the tracking rule was fixed in advance. The frequency drop under the 100 kg preliminary load was barely distinguishable from the measurement error, so the main-test mass was set at 200 kg. With 200 kg placed at mid-span, the frequency
r3-p14-000: fell by 0.6% and returned to its original value after removal; after correcting for amplitude differences, the frequencies with no load, 100 kg and 200 kg lay within error on a single added-mass curve, consistent with an equivalent mass of about 17 t (Figure 7). The model trained on 20 minutes of unloaded walking exceeded the threshold on 18% of windows in the 10 minutes of unloaded walking not used for training, but with no exceedance lasting three or more consecutive windows; during 30 minutes of walking with 200 kg loaded, 46% of windows exceeded and about 32% led to consecutive-3-window alarms (at most 7 consecutive windows). On a single-window basis the separation is weak, since 18% exceeded even without load, but the consecutive-exceedance rate separated the two clearly: the consecutive-window rule filtered out false alarms without missing the change in state. Whether an alarm was caused by mass was established from the drop and recovery of the natural frequency.

r3-p14-004: html:The stage-1 results matched the expected physics. The 8.9% drop in peak frequency for 1-1 is exactly what is expected from the natural frequency falling as mass increases (f = (1/2π)√(k/m)), and for 1-0 the amplitude and band features responded, raising the exceedance rate from 4.5% (normal) to 29.7% and confirming the need for an anomaly score that combines several features. However, the damping of the foam board and the variation of manual tapping made the scatter of normal measurements large, and these two issues became the improvement targets of stage 2.
r3-p14-007: In stage 2, first, standardizing the excitation with a machine fixed the normal baseline: the peaks of all 60 room-temperature normal evaluation windows coincided at 101 Hz within the frequency resolution. Second, the 27 conditions were separated almost completely. The median ratio to threshold was
r3-p14-008: 0.003–0.038× for normal windows and 5.8–73.7× for damage windows, a gap of more than a hundredfold. However, one normal window in the heated block spiked to 15.9× and the weakest damage window reached only 2.0×, so in operation the decision is based on the exceedance rate over consecutive windows. The severity ordering held for mass, with a monotonic increase from M500 5.8× to M1000 22.6× in all three blocks; for bolts alone the score grew from B1 to B2, but combined with mass the ordering reversed (M500·B1 75.4 < M0·B1 264.7), making it hard to use as a severity indicator. Third, the composition of reconstruction-error contributions points to the type of damage (Figure 5). In bolt-loosening windows the 40–80 Hz band-ratio residual accounted for 76–90%, in mass windows the amplitude/energy features for 73–80%, and in combined windows the two groups appeared side by side at 51% and 46%. If the band ratio dominates, the boundary condition (bolts) should be inspected first; if amplitude/energy dominate, the change in load. The stage-1 conclusion that the peak frequency is unstable under mode switching and that features must be combined remained valid. Fourth, the normal training data already covered 22.4–39.9 °C and 48.9–79.0% humidity, so false alarms were rare even without compensation, and the effect of compensation was limited to maintaining recall (100% for all 5 seeds versus 96.2–99.3% uncompensated). The remaining 4 false alarms are windows near the hottest point, 39.9 °C — a limitation of approximating the structure's temperature with air temperature.
r3-p14-009: The largest share of the performance gain came from feature normalization. Because amplitudes differed by up to about 40× between conditions, raw features gave a recall of only 21.3% (0% for mass windows), whereas log and ratio normalization raised it to 100% on the same data.
r3-p15-000: The stage-3 results show four things. First, the system still works when moved to real bridges: on both overpasses the mode peaks were reproduced within 1% and false alarms were low, showing that visit-style inspection with a node moved from bridge to bridge is feasible. Second, the seasonal surge in false alarms reported in prior work [2] did not recur on bridge E because the conditions differed. Z24 used, directly in its decision, a natural frequency that rose sharply as the asphalt layer froze during a year of observation including sub-zero periods. Bridge E differed in both environment and decision method. Environmentally, it was four early-autumn days at 15 °C and above with no frost, so the temperature-driven peak change was only about 0.5%, at the level of the fluctuation between blocks (3.4). In the decision, the autoencoder does not look at frequency directly but compares a score built from eight features with a 99th-percentile threshold, so a frequency shift of a few percent barely shows in the score. In the low-temperature extrapolation of openLAB, whose conditions resemble Z24, the surge reappeared when the frequency channel was combined and was resolved by compensation (2.7). Compensation is therefore needed when the environmental change exceeds the feature scatter and the decision looks at frequency directly, and inputs outside the training range add extrapolation error and should only be flagged. Third, the cause of false alarms on the real bridges was not temperature but excitation conditions such as low amplitude late at night. Bridge E's exceeding windows were dominated by the amplitude/energy group, so the contributions also pointed to a change in excitation, whereas in bridge C's loaded segment the three groups were split evenly and the contributions alone could not identify the cause. Fourth, the frequency drop and recovery under both loads (100 kg and 200 kg) agree with the added-mass formula, so tracking the natural frequency provides the basis for identifying the cause of an alarm.
r3-p15-002: Using only low-cost commercial parts (ADXL355Z, DHT22, Raspberry Pi), this system separated the 27-condition matrix of a laboratory model. The temperature/humidity-compensated model detected all 840 damage windows and raised false alarms on only 4 of 90 normal evaluation windows (recall 100%, false-alarm rate 4.4%, ROC-AUC 0.996), resolving the missed detections of stage 1, where recall was only 0.234, through standardized excitation and feature normalization.
r3-p15-003: Environmental compensation reduced false alarms when training did not cover the environmental variation (stage-1 humidity segment 17.5% → 9.1%; openLAB seasonal extrapolation with the frequency channel combined 26% → 0–3%), with the effect coming mainly from temperature; in stage 2, where the environmental range was covered in advance, it appeared only as maintained recall. In the contribution analysis, the 40–80 Hz band-ratio residual dominated for bolt loosening and the amplitude/energy residuals for mass change, so the alarm alone narrowed the direction of inspection.
r3-p15-004: On the stage-3 real bridges, the mode peaks of both overpasses were tracked within 1% with few false alarms; in the early-autumn field, however, the temperature dependence of the peak was below the noise, so no compensation benefit was confirmed, and false alarms came from insufficient excitation and traffic events. In the added-mass test, a 0.6% frequency drop and recovery under 200 kg was measured, showing that a single low-cost node can distinguish a mass change of about 1% of the mode's equivalent mass (about 17 t). Based on these results, field operation decides with 120-second windows and a rule of three consecutive exceedances, excludes low-amplitude periods without traffic from decisions, and automatically reinitializes the sensor if an error persists for more than a few seconds.
r3-p15-006: Four tasks remain. First, finalize how contributions are reported on real bridges. Because real bridges have no damage labels and the amplitude/energy features depend on traffic volume, the stage-2 correspondence will not be used as is; instead, changes relative to a normal period will be reported by feature group (amplitude, band structure, frequency). Causes will be presented only as candidate starting points for inspection, without judging location or extent (presence detection, level 1 of Rytter's four levels of damage identification [9]), and the contribution profile for each candidate will first be validated on the Z24 data, which include a recorded damage history [3]. Second, re-validate the effect of temperature/humidity compensation by observing for several weeks or more with the same mounting to include sub-zero periods and seasonal transitions, splitting training and evaluation days by date, and securing environmental inputs by shading the air-temperature sensor and pressing the surface-temperature sensor firmly against the deck. Third, integrate the frequency-decision channel (2.7) into the real-time system. Fourth, extend to multiple nodes to estimate the location of damage.
